title: 5 Best Attending Physician Scheduling Software Tools Compared
description: QGenda, Amion, TigerConnect, spreadsheets and Scheduling Wizard compared for attending and faculty scheduling: automation, call fairness and admin burden.
content:
Summary

  • Physician workforce scheduling is a complex task that takes whoever owns it 4-8 hours a month, but optimized systems can increase perceived schedule fairness from 43% to 95%.
  • Most tools either publish the schedule, like Amion, or ask you to build it yourself in a platform like QGenda.
  • The critical choice for program coordinators is between software you must operate and a managed service that delivers a finished schedule.
  • For programs seeking to eliminate the administrative burden, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard builds the finished schedule for you, to your rules.

If you searched "attending physician scheduling software" and landed here, you've probably already noticed something frustrating: most search results return tools built for patient appointment booking, like online intake forms, patient portals, and calendar widgets for scheduling office visits. That's not what you need.

What you're actually looking for is far more complex: a solution for physician workforce scheduling: the intricate, rule-laden process of building Block rotation schedules, Call schedules, and Clinic assignments for a department, group or program, with the ACGME requirements in it where they apply.

These are fundamentally different problems, and conflating them costs you time you don't have.

A note before the list: we are Scheduling Wizard. We build physician schedules as a service, so we have included ourselves below and you should read our entry with that in mind. The order here is by one thing only, who actually builds the schedule, which is why a service comes before software and software comes before a platform you publish through. Rank by cost, or by how good the mobile app is, and the order changes. We have described the other tools as their own users and documentation describe them.

The Real Cost of Getting Physician Scheduling Wrong

Here's what chief residents and program coordinators are actually dealing with:

"It takes at least 4-8 hours a month to make the schedule… and that's before the swaps, tracking fairness, and just carrying it in your head all month. That's what really adds up.", r/hospitalist discussion

And it's not just the time. It's the institutional knowledge that walks out the door every year when the person who built it moves on. It's the ACGME duty hour violations that get caught only after the schedule is already published. Then there's the morale hit when physicians feel the call schedule isn't fair.

That last point matters more than most administrators realize: a published study on PubMed found that switching to an optimized scheduling system boosted residents' perceived fairness of the call schedule from 43% to 95%. That's not a marginal improvement; it's a complete transformation in how your team experiences their work environment.

How We Evaluated These Tools

To cut through the marketing noise, we compared each tool on a consistent rubric:

  • Automation Depth: Does it generate schedules, or just publish them?
  • Call Fairness Distribution: Is fairness built in, or manually tracked?
  • Custom rules: Can it handle GME-specific rules and cross-schedule dependencies?
  • ACGME/Credentialing Compliance: Does it prevent violations, or flag them after the fact?
  • Administrative Burden: How much time and expertise does it require from your team?

With that framework in place, here are the 5 best solutions for attending physician scheduling, a mix of software and managed services.

1. Scheduling Wizard (Managed Service, Not Software)

Best for: departments, provider groups and training programs that want the build off their plate entirely.

Scheduling Wizard is the only entry on this list that isn't self-service software. It's a done-for-you managed scheduling service backed by Y Combinator (W26), built for GME programs, provider groups and practices. Instead of handing you a platform to learn and configure, we write your rules down with you and deliver finished schedules as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you.

You submit your rules (vacation requests, rotation requirements, coverage rules, resident preferences) and receive the finished block, call, clinic and attending schedules, built to your rules. No logins. No configuration. No learning curve.

Rubric Rating
Automation Depth Fully managed, zero software to operate
Call Fairness Distribution Built for fair call, weekend, and holiday distribution
Custom rules Cross-schedule dependencies resolved in the build
ACGME Compliance The rules are applied as we build, not flagged afterwards
Administrative Burden Zero, programs never touch a scheduling platform

The key differentiator: Unlike every other option on this list, Scheduling Wizard solves the institutional continuity problem. When your chief resident rotates out, the scheduling knowledge doesn't leave with them. The service provides continuity year after year.

Programs that already use Amion or QGenda for day-to-day schedule viewing often use Scheduling Wizard alongside them: SW builds the optimized schedule, then the program puts the finished schedule into its existing publishing platform.

What you get: the finished schedule as an Excel or Google Sheets file, or on a custom live view we build for the group. Redrafts come with it: when a partner's availability changes or a site shifts its coverage, we rebuild rather than hand you a correction exercise. For the specifics, see attending physician scheduling software.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Best for: Groups whose coverage rules and contract terms change faster than a platform can be reconfigured.

Attending coverage is still mostly built in spreadsheets, including at departments that own an enterprise platform. That is why it is second. A spreadsheet takes contract terms, site splits, partner preferences and the handshake agreements that never got written down, and it takes them immediately. Sheets lets the whole group see the same version.

The trade is that fairness is whatever the person counting says it is. Call equity across a year is an arithmetic problem, and arithmetic done by hand under time pressure is where disputes start.

Why the middle is harder than it looks. A rules-based platform will hand back a generated schedule, and that feels like the work is done. In practice someone then checks it against the requirements, fixes what it missed, and discovers the fixes cascade. Programs in that position frequently keep a separate spreadsheet for equity, which is a fair sign of where the real work still lives.

3. QGenda

Best for: Large health systems with dedicated administrative staff and IT resources.

QGenda is one of the most widely recognized names in physician workforce management. It's a complete, enterprise-grade SaaS platform that goes beyond scheduling to include credentialing, time tracking, and analytics, all in one system.

But "complete" comes with a caveat. As one physician put it in an online forum: "Getting QG to actually do what you want isn't easy, and learning how it works is very complicated." That sentiment is common, QGenda is powerful, but it demands a dedicated administrator who has the time and expertise to configure and maintain it.

Rubric Rating
Automation Depth Self-service, rules and templates must be built and managed by your team
Call Fairness Distribution Trackable, but fairness depends entirely on how accurately you configure the rules
Custom rules Flexible setup, but complex GME schedules require extensive user configuration
ACGME Compliance Flags violations after the fact, does not prevent them during schedule generation
Administrative Burden High, steep learning curve and ongoing maintenance required

QGenda makes the most sense for large health systems that have the administrative bandwidth to manage the platform and want a single integrated tool for all workforce operations. For an already-stretched chief resident or program coordinator, it can become another burden rather than a relief.

4. Amion

Best for: Programs that need a simple, low-cost way to publish and share a finished schedule.

Amion is ubiquitous in academic medicine, but it's important to understand what it actually does. Amion is fundamentally a schedule publishing platform, not a schedule generation tool. You build the schedule somewhere else (usually Excel), then input it into Amion so your physicians can view it from their phones or computers.

There's nothing wrong with that. For what it does, Amion does it well. But it does not reduce the core administrative burden of creating a fair, compliant, finished schedule, that work still happens entirely outside the platform.

Rubric Rating
Automation Depth None, all scheduling is manual and happens outside Amion
Call Fairness Distribution None, no fairness tracking or enforcement features
Custom rules None, no rule configuration or custom rule handling
ACGME Compliance None, no duty hour tracking or violation flagging
Administrative Burden Low for publishing tasks, but does not address the burden of building the schedule

Amion is the last mile of your scheduling workflow, not the solution to it. Many programs use it in combination with a more solid creation tool or service.

5. TigerConnect Physician Scheduling

Best for: Hospitals already using TigerConnect for clinical communication.

TigerConnect is primarily known as a clinical communication and collaboration (CC&C) platform for secure messaging, alerts, and care team coordination. Their physician scheduling module is an add-on that integrates directly with that communication layer, meaning on-call notifications and schedule updates flow into the same system your team already uses for messaging.

As a standalone attending physician scheduling software, it's a capable self-service tool with rule-based automation and shift-request management. But like QGenda, it puts the configuration and maintenance burden squarely on your administrator.

Rubric Rating
Automation Depth Self-service with rule-based draft generation, requires administrator management
Call Fairness Distribution Trackable, but dependent on careful and accurate user configuration
Custom rules Handles common rules; primarily optimized for communication integration
ACGME Compliance Post-creation compliance checking, violations flagged, not prevented
Administrative Burden Moderate to high, requires learning the platform and managing ongoing scheduling

If your organization is already embedded in the TigerConnect ecosystem, the scheduling module is a natural fit. If you're evaluating it as a standalone scheduling solution, the integration value diminishes and the self-service burden becomes harder to justify.

The Decision Guide: Software to Run, or a Schedule That's Done?

Every tool on this list falls into one of three categories, and knowing which category matches your actual need will save you months of frustration.

Publishing platforms (Amion): Necessary for communicating a finished schedule to your team. Not useful for building one. If you already have a schedule creation process and just need a clean way to publish it, Amion is your answer.

Self-Service Platforms (QGenda, TigerConnect): These put a powerful system in your hands, and that's exactly the problem. The burden of learning, configuring, and maintaining the platform falls on an already-overworked chief resident or coordinator. These tools work well when you have dedicated administrative staff with the time and expertise to manage them. For most residency programs, that's not reality.

Managed Service (Scheduling Wizard): This is the only model where the operator burden disappears entirely. You don't learn software. You don't configure rules. You submit your rules, and you receive the finished schedule, built to them. When your chief rotates out, the institutional knowledge stays with the service.

In short:

If you need a tool to publish and share a schedule you've already built, use Amion or QGenda.

If you need someone to actually build the schedule for you, to your rules, Scheduling Wizard is the only managed service on this list.

The right attending physician scheduling software isn't always software. Sometimes it's the right team, and a finished schedule waiting in your inbox.

Frequently Asked Questions

What's the difference between physician workforce scheduling and patient scheduling software?

Physician workforce scheduling software is designed to build complex staff schedules based on rules and requests, while patient scheduling software is for booking patient appointments. The tools you need for creating a fair and ACGME-compliant call schedule for dozens of residents are fundamentally different from a calendar widget that lets a patient book an office visit online.

How does a managed service like Scheduling Wizard differ from software like QGenda?

A managed scheduling service builds the schedule for you and delivers a finished product, while scheduling software provides a complex tool that your team must learn, configure, and operate themselves. The managed service model eliminates the administrative burden and steep learning curve associated with self-service platforms.

How can I ensure my residency schedule is ACGME compliant?

Put the rules into the schedule while it is built, rather than flagging violations after a schedule exists. The review at the end then has far less to find.

How does Scheduling Wizard handle complex ACGME rules for specific subspecialties?

Scheduling Wizard handles subspecialty-specific ACGME rules by having our schedulers write your program’s rules down and build to them. Whether it's the unique duty hour requirements for surgery, the clinic demands of internal medicine, or call frequency rules for anesthesiology, the requirements you tell us apply are part of the build.

Did the February 2026 ACGME revision change the work hour rules?

Less than the headlines suggested. The February 2026 interim revision of the Common Program Requirements did not change the work hour limits; it suspended enforcement of a handful of requirements, including the rotation-specific 88-hour exception, while the ACGME prepares a major revision (a draft was posted for comment in September 2026 with a proposed effective date of July 1, 2028; nothing in it applies yet). The rules a schedule is built to today are the ones in place since the 2017 revision: 80 hours a week averaged over four weeks, with clinical work from home, at-home call activity and moonlighting all counted; no more than 24 hours of continuous scheduled work plus up to four for transitions, at every PGY level; at least 14 hours free after 24 hours of in-house call; one day in seven free, averaged over four weeks, with no at-home call on those days; and in-house call no more often than every third night. We build to the rules in force, and when they change we rebuild to the new ones.

Can I use Scheduling Wizard if my program already uses Amion?

Yes, absolutely. Scheduling Wizard is designed to work alongside tools like Amion and QGenda. Our service delivers a complete, optimized schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. You then simply upload that finished schedule to your existing platform, which continues to be the daily viewing and communication tool for your residents and faculty.

What happens when our chief resident leaves? How is scheduling knowledge retained?

Managed scheduling services solve the institutional continuity problem by retaining all your program's rules, preferences, and scheduling history externally. When a chief resident rotates out, the knowledge of how to build your complex schedule doesn't leave with them. The service provides year-over-year stability and consistency, onboarding the new chief with an established, proven process.
